subject: physics

moments.title: Onnes discovers superconductivity
moments.body:
Onnes had been the first to liquefy helium in 1908, reaching 4.2 K. He measures the resistance of mercury as it cools. At 4.2 K, the resistance drops suddenly to ZERO — unmeasurably low.

Mercury becomes a superconductor. Onnes wins the 1913 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: Some materials lose all electrical resistance below a critical temperature. Mechanism unknown.

moments.title: Meissner effect
moments.who: Walther Meissner and Robert Ochsenfeld, Berlin
moments.body:
Meissner and Ochsenfeld discover that a superconductor doesn't merely allow current to flow without resistance — it actively expels magnetic fields from its interior. This is the Meissner effect: superconductors are PERFECT diamagnets.

This is more than 'zero resistance' (which would lock in any pre-existing field). It's a genuine new state of matter.
moments.takeaway: Superconductivity is a distinct thermodynamic phase — not just very-good conductivity.

moments.title: BCS theory
moments.who: Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer, University of Illinois
moments.body:
Bardeen (who had already won one Nobel for the transistor), Leon Cooper and J. Robert Schrieffer publish a microscopic theory of superconductivity. Electrons in a superconductor pair up ('Cooper pairs') via lattice vibrations and condense into a single quantum state.

The theory wins a 1972 Nobel — Bardeen's second. He is the only person to win two Nobel Prizes in Physics.
moments.takeaway: Superconductivity is a macroscopic quantum effect. Electrons cooperate via lattice vibrations to form pairs that flow without resistance.

moments.title: High-temperature superconductivity
moments.body:
BCS theory predicted a ceiling of about 30 K for superconductivity. Bednorz and Müller find ceramic copper oxides (cuprates) that superconduct at 35 K, then 90 K (above liquid nitrogen, 77 K) — vastly easier and cheaper to cool.

The 1987 Nobel comes a year after publication — fastest Nobel ever for a physics discovery. Mechanism is still not fully understood. Cuprates don't obey BCS theory cleanly.
moments.takeaway: A new class of superconductors works above the BCS ceiling. Theory is left behind by experiment.

moments.title: Hydride superconductors at near-room temperature, high pressure
moments.body:
Sulfur hydrides, lanthanum hydrides and other 'hydride' compounds show superconductivity above 200 K — but only at million-atmosphere pressures.

Claims of room-temperature superconductivity at lower pressures (carbonaceous sulfur hydride, 2020; LK-99, 2023) have been retracted or failed replication. The field is active, contested, and sometimes embarrassing.
moments.takeaway: Higher-temperature superconductors keep appearing — but practical room-temperature, ambient-pressure superconductivity remains elusive.

now.title: Superconductors today
now.body:
Superconductors are used in MRI scanners, particle accelerators (LHC magnets), MagLev trains and high-precision instruments (SQUIDs). Quantum computers built on superconducting qubits (Google, IBM) leverage Cooper-pair physics directly.

The field still has fundamental mysteries: the cuprates' mechanism, the iron pnictides, the rich phenomenology of pairing symmetries.
now.open_questions: Is room-temperature, ambient-pressure superconductivity possible? What's the mechanism in cuprates? Can we design superconductors using machine learning + computation? What new states of matter lurk near the superconducting transition?

reflection: John Bardeen is the only person to win two Nobel Prizes in Physics — for the transistor and for BCS theory. He was famously low-key, even shy. How does a single person produce two field-defining works? And why did Marie Curie (the only person with Nobels in two different sciences) win such different recognition for it?
